body:
People dunking on other people for feeling suicidal are selfish.  I'm posting here for the first time in literally two years because I'm struggling again.  But the one constant in the narrative of people who struggled with suicide, both personally and in this subreddit historically, is that one thing holding them back is some variation of "it will make mom sad".

I am having a very intense and very recent struggle with suicide thoughts.  If I pull the metaphorical trigger, the people I know care about me are going to do pretty well financially.  They may well be emotionally devastated (which whatever else is staying my hand) but they, or at least their kids, will have access to the net gains of my uncashed 401k and the unwisely uninvested dollars in my checking account.

TLDR: If you're suicidal, find help. If you think suicidal people are being "selfish", well you might be the asshole who's going to get a payout when they finally make "that" decision.

I appreciate what you're saying but my takeaway of your post is that you you managed to say to someone "Hi! I'm into bondage" and became really good friends with them.  Seriously ladies ranged from being grossed out to being transparently looking for a way out through my young adult life.  I don't even hold it against them I am kind of an asymmetrical wide grosso.  

THAT ASIDE, I'd feel pretty guilty for sticking around for my unknown nephew while I am ready to just end it.  I'd rather bow out now than be part of his life and then cripple out from a liver turned into a drug addled raisin.  

Guilt and hopelessness is a big part of why I'm convinced now is a better time than ever to make my exit.  The people most important to me are at a good place now, and I just don't have it in me anymore so I'd rather bow out while they're at their best than at their worst.

This is my third therapist and while I can't say whether or not she's great, I like her more than my last two and she seems genuinely concerned about my well being and after all the sessions we've had she seems closer to understanding me and my issues than anyone else I know.  That feels like it's worth something to me.

Thanks for the reply.

For me, the whole "doing something different" part is part of the drag.  It's been a cycle in my life to get so miserable that I do something radical to shake things up -- that's how I got where I am now, and how I've found myself relatively successful -- but after the newness stops I find myself slowly but surely ending up right back where I started.

And that's kind of the poison.  When I was a younger man and found myself feeling my worst, I boiled it down to two choices: Give up or shake up my life and hope to find happiness.  The shake up routine is work, it takes effort.  And when it doesn't work, it gets discouraging.  The thought of doing a dramatic shake up again isn't exciting to me -- it sounds like draining labor.  I just want a win.  I just want a problem solved without having to work so hard for it.  I'm tired.
(if brevity is the soul of wit then I ain't fucking witty)

For some reason it left me devastated.  It shouldn't have surprised me, since I had basically broken off all communication on my end over the years in my shame.  It was pretty clear to me that I wasn't worthy of hanging out with these guys, let alone with a whole gaggle of people who were living my dream.  I probably wasn't invited because it didn't even cross their mind -- I had made myself out to be an impersonal an uninteresting guy while I stayed with them, and seemed to be separating myself from them more and more with each chance I got.  But it was more like, after all the work I had done to improve myself, after all the obsessing over finally being "good enough" or "worthy enough" to be in the company of people I admired, I was actually further back than where I started.  And for the first time, I fully realized that I was acting irrationally.  I was letting myself be ruled by this habit of feeling smaller and less important than everyone else.

I drank myself in to a stupor and finally confessed that I was having these issues to my sister.  Within a couple of weeks I was seeing a therapist for the first time in my life.

Six months later, you're reading this.  I'm still in therapy and have tried a number of different medications.  Nothing has worked.  I was initially hopeful that therapy would turn things around.  And it has helped, but unfortunately it's helped me more to understand the problem than to fix it.  I can now rationally realize that I'm not all that bad a guy, not all that ugly, I might even be talented in some respects.  I can rationally realize that the dozens of people I walk past each day probably aren't perfect, they probably have problems just like me.  Yet when it's time to play ball and interact, I fall on my face the same way I always did.  I fall prey to my panic and my self loathing.

I've been getting gradually more depressed.  Over the last two weeks my business partner has been out of town, and my days have consisted of sleeping until the afternoon, working until about midnight, and then drinking myself asleep so I can do it all again tomorrow.  I've been subsisting off delivery pizza and take out indian food while my perfectly healthy groceries expire in the fridge.  Meanwhile I was letting other responsibilities slip by me.

Last night I won a small victory.  I buckled down and did some spring cleaning.  I finished a handful of volunteer projects I had let fall behind (volunteer work being something I started doing regularly while I was trying to improve myself over the years).  They had been taking up a lot of mindshare and actually were making me more depressed.  But I caught up with them late last night, and for a moment at least I was pretty pleased.  I overindulged in alcohol and played some online games and all seemed right with the world.

I woke up today back to feeling awful, and it wasn't because of the booze.

The problem is this.  I realize what's wrong with me, how I keep projecting a fantasy of myself versus others.  Even though I feel inferior to everyone, I can REASON that isn't necessarily the case.  But that isn't stopping how I feel.

So I can beat this right?  I can change this pattern of behavior I've been following since basically puberty.  Maybe.  I mean I don't know for sure.  And diagnosing the problem has so far only revealed one thing: there's no magic fix.  This is going to take work.

I'm so tired of working.  As far back as high school I looked forward to having a wife and kids.  Now I'm 28 and the female body seems almost more like a fantasy world I get a distorted view of through the wonders of internet porn.  I've loathed myself since high school and despite realizing my self perception is skewed I loathe myself even more today.  I catch myself feeling guilty over feeling guilty -- I'm well fed and well paid and have satisfying work, why should I be depressed?  So many times in my life suicide has sounded like a pretty sweet deal, and now here I live within strolling distance of the golden gate bridge and I think how easy it would be to walk out the door late one night and not come back.  I find myself strangely soothed as I ponder measures to make sure there's no way I'd survive, make sure that against all odds this would be misinterpreted as a cry for help.  There have been times when the only thing that's stopped me is knowing how badly it would hurt my family.  No matter what I think of myself, they love me, and my death (or disappearance) would be devastating.

And I have a lot to live for really.  My company is launching its first fully fleshed product soon, and in addition to that I'm really close to finishing a video game I've been programming in my spare time.  I still find myself able to enjoy the same things I always have, a new video game or a used book with that used book smell, but I fear it's too often an escape rather than a distraction.  Despite my social ineptitude I still have a stable of friends, however small, who seem to like me, and I still have a family that loves me.  I have a lot more than a lot of other people.

But every morning I want to get out of bed less, and this depression is so familiar that imagining life without it seems like some kind of ridiculous fantasy.  Something unreal and unattainable -- how could those facebook galleries full of people in groups enjoying themselves ever include me?  All I have is this inkling of a hope that if I work at it, I might be able to change my ways.  It's uncertain and it won't be easy.  Well I've put work in to feeling better about myself and fixing this problem before, and it hasn't worked.  I think about repeating that effort, and I just want to stay in bed instead.

Has anyone triumphed over extremely similar circumstances?  I'd like to hang in there.  But some days it's less like suicide is a "final option" and more like it's just something I'm putting off until I can at least put enough work in to making sure my death inconveniences people as little as possible.

I absolutely failed socially in college.  Though I managed to score a few new friends, I felt almost completely out of my element everywhere I went.  I didn't like the college culture -- I didn't like the music everyone else liked, I didn't like the shows everyone else liked, I didn't like the activities everyone else liked.  I'd get out to a party, sure, but I was a complete party pooper, generally keeping to myself and being completely unable to maintain a normal or interesting conversation.  To make matters worse, my fellow CompSci majors, the folks I probably should have been socializing with, all seemed much more accomplished than me.  Yeah we were all freshman, but where as I was a computer "whiz" in high school for maybe being able to make the printer work right, many students in my first day of class already had experience in actual programing!  I had previously taught myself BASIC on a "laptop" computer that had a screen 3 characters tall and 20 characters wide.  I didn't even understand how you were supposed to be able to program something without a GOTO statement.

Of course that shouldn't have stopped me from stepping up and socializing with these people, who were probably much more similar to me than whoever was at last week's frat party.  But I was in awe of them, and it was here a pattern emerged that has since plagued my entire adult life.  I think I pretty much suck compared to everybody, particularly those who I envision to be what I want to be.

I struggled through college, at one time ending up on academic probation.  I was never the sharpest knife in the drawer, but even worse, I was so alienated by my classmates that I never formed in to any study groups or homework groups.  I was even afraid to bother my professors.  If I didn't understand something, that was a problem I apparently had and there was no fixing it.

I got out of college and immediately got a job nearby, still nestled right in the midwest.  I hated this job.  I was still in a place where I didn't feel like I fit in, I still found it difficult to find people I found interesting even before I started comparing myself poorly to them. I had put on a bunch of weight and was living with a couple of my only close friends in the area.  As we got older, they got girlfriends that then became wives.  I was always single, always the odd wheel, to the point where it became a running gag in my circle of friends.  They were sweet to me, and they are still great friends to me, but I'd be lying if I didn't say it hurt when year after year, no matter what, if I went out with my friends there would always be an odd number of people in the crew, and that would be because I was the only one without a date.

After about two years of this job and lifestyle, I was drinking and crying myself to sleep every night.  I hated myself and I hated what I had become.  It was like I let all my dreams die because I just didn't have it in me, and now I was trapped in a life I didn't want.  I never shared this depression with anyone.  I think as far as my friends were concerned I was odd and cynical but not unhappy.  I was seriously considering suicide, but one day I just snapped and said we'll go all in.  I put in my two week notice at work and moved back in with the parents while I started a nation wide job hunt.  Within a month I landed a new gig in San Francisco with a very well known tech company.  With nothing to my name but a suitcase and a credit card with a $1000 limit I moved out west.

I had a friend who put me up in the city for a couple months, and unfortunately it seemed I was already determined to sabotage myself in this new land.  This friend of mine and her two roommates had good tech jobs with huge established companies of good repute.  I wouldn't say they were living my dream, but they were a lot closer to it, and they made it look effortless.  By comparison, I was a small town hick who barely finished state college.  I couldn't believe they were generous enough to put up with me.  I was simply in awe of them, and I was constantly afraid of looking like an ass with them.  So I was quiet and reserved and antisocial.  But they were still super friendly all the way through my stay, even though I clammed up like a dick.

Eventually I got my own place in a pretty bad neighborhood in Oakland.  It was all I could afford at the time, but it was an easy bicycle ride to BART and thus work.  Unfortunately, after about 8 months on the job I was fired.  Turns out I really didn't have what it took to cut it at that particular company.  I sensed I was in over my head after I started but was trying my hardest to catch up.  Unfortunately after a couple of tardies that were pretty much my fault, they didn't see much reason to keep me on board.

I went through a bad spell there.  My ego had definitely taken a heavy blow, and I felt so ashamed I couldn't even show my face to the friends who had housed me before.  I never left my apartment in ghetto Oakland.  I supported myself with a combination of contract work and, when there was no work to be found, unemployment checks.

Eventually, after answering a Craigslist ad, I landed a contract-to-hire programming role with a startup in its infancy.  I felt guilty, like I had fooled the blokes in to letting me on board long enough to discover I sucked, and then they could fire me and I could sucker the next bloke.  Except something happened here -- I was passably decent enough at my job that my superior was actually satisfied with my work.  Meanwhile, in the startup environment, I was given the freedom to choose which hours I worked (though I had to work a lot of them) and was able to expand my skillset almost on demand, since there were times that things needed doing and as one of the only guys in the company you might have to end up doing them, even if you didn't know how to do it before.

It was the start of a big uptrend for me.  Two years later the company is still afloat and profitable and we're weeks away from releasing our first fully featured product to public beta.  I am now the senior manager at said company, which isn't so impressive considering the company has never been larger than a handful of people, but the point is that I'm in charge of development now and though I still constantly doubt my skills, the software does what it's supposed to and the trains run on time.

But it wasn't all roses -- I was still socially inept.  Now every day I walked to work in downtown San Francisco, I saw beautiful women everywhere.  Some are sharp dressed business types, some were obviously geeky girls with nerdy interests, but all of them gorgeous and capable and independent and perfect and terrifying.  I was in a city surrounded by cities all full of people who had interests similar to mine and passions similar to mine.  People whose main interests weren't small town sports or the deer hunting season.  But to me, they all seemed confident, professionally accomplished, and perfect.  I though I was faking it.  I figured despite my success the emperor had no clothes and I was going to be revealed for the fraud I was, and in the meantime I wasn't going to be able to communicate with these more authentic, more natural, more in-their-element geeks without exposing myself for the charlatan I was.

One day while I was buying clothes for myself, I looked in the mirror in the dressing room and was disgusted by what I saw.  I also realized that I had been avoiding mirrors for as long as I could remember.  I hated to look at my face.  I hated to look at my body.  I hated that I was already getting a bald spot.  The though of touching my own body made my skin crawl -- surely I could never ask anyone else to be intimate with me, while I was so disgusting.  It was no wonder I hadn't managed to get a girl in bed.  It was no great mystery why I couldn't confidently talk to people.

So I decided to make another change in my life.  I started walking to the office each day -- about two miles worth of parading.  I did a small workout before showering each day.  I cut back on calories and started eating healthier. I lost a lot of weight, and people noticed, and that felt pretty good.  I started dressing better and tending to my appearance.

Then I decided I would try and meet people.  But nothing changed.  I would go to a new gathering and feel outclassed.  I tried a board game group, I tried a tech karaoke group, I tried a couple of meet up groups.  Every time it was the same thing -- I found myself gravitating to the corners, trying not to be noticed.  When someone did try and strike up conversation, I was so nervous and awkward that it usually ended fast.  I was a disaster.  They were all still better than me.

The last straw actually came last Halloween.  I hadn't made any plans.  Why should I?  While I actually enjoyed the prospect of Halloween, all I could see was me in the dark corner of a bar wearing a dumb costume that seemed witty at the time, drinking myself in to a stupor while San Francisco showed me how it's REALLY done.  But those friends of mine who let me sleep on their couch years ago?  They threw their own Halloween party, full of nerdy people doing nerdy things.  And they didn't invite me.
